t: the borrower. One who receives an object from his fellow to use without payment.

or the animal was broken. For example, it was injured by a wild animal or damaged in another way (see Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael and Mekhilta de-Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai on Exodus 22:9 and the Bible commentators there).
when it was beyond his control not at the time of work. When the object or animal was lost to circumstances beyond control not during the work for which it was borrowed.
or rode on it or threshed with it etc.. Since he borrowed it for plowing and changed and used it for other work, even if it died during the work, he is liable.
an axe to split wood with. An axe to chop pieces of wood.
he should bring proof etc.. Where people are present he must bring witnesses as to what happened, and cannot be exempted by an oath (see Hilchot Sechirut 3:1).
and that he did not change it. That he did not make a use that he did not agree on in advance with the lender.
to draw water with it inside his ruin. He borrowed the animal to do a certain job inside the ruin, which is a place where no one sees.

in the way that damages are assessed. Just as one who causes damage pays only the difference between what the thing was worth before the damage and what it is worth now, and returns what remains of it to the owner (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 7:8).
from the moment he drew it. The Sages enacted that the borrowing begins at the moment the borrower draws the object or animal (see Hilchot Sechirut 2:8).
and if its flesh wasted away. Its flesh dwindled during the borrowing period, not because of the work.
he must pay. Just as he is responsible for the loss of the entire animal, so he is responsible for partial loss.
without specification. Without a fixed period having been agreed on in advance.
the lender may take it back whenever he wishes. He may take the object back at any time (unlike an ordinary loan, which he may not demand for thirty days - see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 13:5).
and it is logical. This can be learned by reasoning.

the buyer etc.. A buyer and a recipient of a gift are parallel to a renter and a borrower: the buyer and the recipient of a gift receive the object entirely, for payment or free, and a renter and borrower receive the object for a set time, for payment or free. And just as the law of the giver of a gift is the same as that of the seller, in that he cannot retract, so the law of the lender is like that of the lessor, who cannot retract within the agreed time.

their father left them. If the borrower died, his sons are entitled to continue the borrowing, but they do not have the law of a borrower who is liable for circumstances beyond control, because they did not accept responsibility as a borrower. They are, however, liable for theft and loss, for they have the law of a paid custodian, since they use the cow and benefit (Sma 341:8).
they estimated. They mistakenly thought.

they pay the price of meat at the cheap rate. According to its cheap rate, which is two thirds of the market price at that time (see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 6:23). They pay only what they benefited, not the full damage caused to the owner (compare Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 3:2).

and if their father left them property etc.. The father's property that the orphans inherited is encumbered for the father's debts (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:7 and ibid. halakhah 11). And here, from the moment the father borrowed the object, the property was encumbered for payment of any circumstance beyond control that may occur in the future.

the lender cannot take it back from him etc.. After the borrower has drawn the object, the lender cannot take it back before the borrower does the work for which he borrowed the vessel, like the law of a borrower for a fixed time.
was worn down. Was worn out (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 11:3).
the handle. The handle.
if they made a kinyan from the lender regarding this. They performed a kinyan sudar (symbolic acquisition) to give force to the agreement (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
and the borrower may not go back and repair the vessel or remake it. For he lent him only this vessel as it is.
a trough. A pit or well that was prepared for watering animals or irrigating fields.
and it was destroyed. Until it was unfit for use.
he cannot rebuild it. In order to continue using it until the end of the borrowing period, because he lent him this particular trough.
he may rebuild it. Since he did not lend him a specific trough, the borrowing did not end when the first trough was destroyed.
he said to him, "lend me a place for a trough". He asked him to lend land in order to build a trough on it.
for lodging, not less than one day etc.. See Hilchot Sechirut 6:6 and the commentary there.
a cloak. An outer garment.
to go in it to a house of mourning. To comfort the mourners.
enough time to go and return. For comforters do not usually stay long at the house of mourning.
to a house of feasting, that entire day. For people stay a long time at the home of the bride and groom.
to make his own feast in it, not less than seven days. For the days of the groom and bride's feast last seven days.
one who borrows along with the owner. That at the time of borrowing, the owner of the object is borrowed or hired for work for him.

provided that the owner was borrowed first or together with the object. That before he borrowed the object from the owner, or at the time of borrowing, he asked the owner to do a certain job for him without payment, so that the owner is borrowed to work for him; then he is exempt even if the owner is not doing the work for him at the time the object is damaged.
as we have explained. Hilchot Sechirut 1:3.
whether he borrowed the owners or hired them. Whether he asked them to do the work for him without payment or hired them to do it.
this is a borrowing along with the owner, and he is exempt. For the owner was borrowed by him for the purpose of watering before he lent him the animal.

he lent his animal or hired it out etc.. That the exemption of "its owner is with it" applies not only in borrowing along with the owner but also in hiring and in all forms of guarding (as explained at the end of the chapter and in Hilchot Sechirut 1:3).
for a load. To carry a burden.
to assist. To help.
this is guarding along with the owner. Since at the time of the borrowing or hiring, the owner assisted the borrower or hirer.
to inspect. To supervise.
it is not guarding along with the owner. Since he did not do it for the borrower or hirer but to guard his own animal.
a teacher of children etc.. All of these are at the service of the townspeople at set times.
and one who plants for the townspeople. Plants trees for the people of the town.
and one who lets their blood. For medical purposes.
and their scribe. For writing documents and the like.

on the day he sits to engage in his work etc.. Since on that day he is available to do work for the townspeople, even if he is not actually engaged in work, if they borrow or hire something from him this is guarding along with the owner (Maggid Mishneh, Yad Pashut; and see the rulings and views).
a teacher. One who teaches, a reciter.
and they were fixed to come always. They come to learn with him on a regular basis.
and he moves for them from tractate to tractate. He moves on of his own accord from tractate to tractate and does not need their consent.

they are borrowed by him. Just as the students need the teacher, so the teacher needs students to help him in study. And when the teacher sets the subject of study, they are as if borrowed by him to help him in his study (Even HaAzel, and see Meiri, Bava Metzia 97a).
and on the day of the pereq. When they expound the laws of the approaching festival.

he is borrowed by them and they are not borrowed by him. On this day he may not change the subject as he wishes and is bound to the students to teach them a particular matter, so he is considered borrowed by them (Meiri, ibid.). Some explain that on the day of the pereq other people come to hear the teacher, and he is bound to the public to expound on the subject of the festival, so he is considered borrowed by the whole public (Even HaAzel).
one who says to his agent, "go and borrow". That at the time of borrowing the animal, the owner appointed an agent to do work for the borrower.

for the hand of the slave is like the hand of his master. The body of a Canaanite slave is acquired by his master, and the slave's hand is considered as the owner's hand, as if the owner himself were borrowed by the borrower (see also below 3:1).
without his master's knowledge it is not a borrowing along with the owner. The slave's hand is considered his master's hand only with the master's consent.

one who borrows from a woman and her husband is borrowed to him. He borrowed from a wife property whose fruits her husband is entitled to eat and whose profits he enjoys (melog property), and at the same time borrowed her husband to do work for him.

it is not a borrowing along with the owner, for acquisition of the fruits is not like acquisition of the body, and the husband has only the fruits. The husband's right to the fruits is not considered ownership of the body of the property, so he borrowed only from the wife and not from her husband, and this is not a borrowing along with the owner.

one who borrows from his wife. A wife does work for her husband and is obligated to do certain tasks for him (see Hilchot Ishut chapter 21), so if he borrowed property belonging to her, it is considered a borrowing along with the owner.
partners who borrowed from one another. They are together and work for one another in the partnership business.

and if one partner said to his fellow, "lend me today and I will lend you tomorrow," it is not a borrowing along with the owner. Even though they are partners, when each one takes it upon himself to work alone in the partnership business one day and his fellow one day, on this day they are not considered partners and this is not a borrowing along with the owner (see Kesef Mishneh in the name of the glosses of Maharam of Padua, and Yad Pashut).
borrowed from the partners and one of them was borrowed to him. He borrowed an object belonging to partners, and one of the partners was borrowed to do work for the borrower.
and likewise partners who borrowed and one of them was borrowed to him. The partners borrowed an object from him and he was borrowed to do work for one of them.
therefore if it died he does not pay. Since there is doubt here, we follow the rule that the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract, so the owners cannot extract money from the borrower.

and if the owners seized, we do not take it from their hands. If the owners seized the borrower's money for the animal that died, they are now in possession of the money, and the borrower who wants to extract it from them must bring proof.

the custodian was negligent with it, he pays. Although in an ordinary case of borrowing along with the owner he is exempt even for negligence, when we are in doubt whether the case is considered borrowing along with the owner, one who was negligent pays. For a negligent person is like one who causes damage, so if he was negligent he is liable unless it is certain that the law of guarding along with the owner applies to him (Maggid Mishneh, and see Yad Pashut).
for mating. To mate the animal.
or to be seen with it. To look wealthy, and not to use it.
or to do with it less than a perutah's worth. That the value of the work the animal will do is less than a perutah.
or he borrowed two cows to do with them a perutah's worth. So each cow by itself does work worth less than a perutah.

all of these are a doubtful borrowing along with the owner. There is doubt whether these uses are defined as work, and the exemption of borrowing along with the owner applies only when the object and the owner are borrowed for doing work (Meiri, Bava Metzia 96a).
borrowed along with the owner etc.. Before he returned it to the lender, he hired it from him. And at the beginning of the hire it was not a borrowing along with the owner.

for the hire depends on the borrowing. Since in hiring he does not take on additional responsibility that was not present at the stage of borrowing, there is no need for a new commitment. So responsibility in the hire depends on the commitment that existed at the time of the borrowing, which was along with the owner.
and afterwards she married. And when she married, her property passed to her husband's use, and among it was the thing she had borrowed.

the husband is like a buyer from her. The Sages enacted that the husband's status regarding his wife's property is that of a purchaser and not a custodian who is liable. And since he thought the animal belonged to the wife, he did not accept any responsibility of guarding, and he is exempt even if he was negligent with it.
and the woman must pay. Since her responsibility toward the lender remains in force.
when she has the means to pay. For example, when she becomes a widow or is divorced.
he steps into her place. Since he knew it was borrowed, responsibility for the animal rests on him.
all that we have said etc.. See also Hilchot Sechirut 1:3.

in the hand of the borrower's agent. A person who is generally accepted by the borrower as an agent (but if he appointed him to be an agent for this matter, it enters his domain from the time it comes to his hand, as explained later in the halakhah - compare Hilchot Gezelah 7:10).
and it died before it entered the borrower's domain, he is exempt. For as long as the cow did not reach the borrower's domain it is still under the lender's responsibility.
he is liable. When the borrower agreed to receive the cow through an agent, it enters his domain and comes under the borrower's responsibility from the time it reaches the agent's hand.
in the hand of his Canaanite slave. Of the lender.
struck it. Hit it.
the borrower is not liable for it. Even though the lender struck it at his request, since it had not yet entered his domain.
he sent it with his Canaanite slave. Of the borrower.
if he returned it within the days of its borrowing. For example, he borrowed it until a certain time and returned it to him before that time arrived.
and he is like a paid custodian over it. Since he benefited from it all the days of the borrowing, he is like one who received payment for the cow he is now guarding.
therefore if it died or was captured after the days of its borrowing, he is exempt. Like the law of a paid custodian, who is exempt for circumstances beyond control.
borrowed one and hired one. Received for his use two cows, one by borrowing and one by hiring.
the lender says, "the borrowed one died" etc.. And the borrower is liable for circumstances beyond control and must pay him.
or the custodian said, "the hired one died" etc.. And the hirer is exempt from paying for circumstances beyond control.
the one who seeks to extract from his fellow bears the burden of proof. And the borrower is exempt from paying until the owner of the cow brings proof of his claim.
this one says hired and that one says borrowed. This is another case, in which both parties claim with certainty.

the custodian swears about the hired one that it died naturally, as he claimed etc.. He swears the custodians' oath by Torah law that the animal died naturally, as with any custodian, and the oath is extended to include that it was the hired one that died and not the borrowed one (see Kesef Mishneh, Beit Yosef, Even HaAzel and Yad Pashut, who discussed the relationship between the form of the oath in this case and the first three cases mentioned in the preceding paragraph, and whether there too it is the custodians' oath or a lesser oath).
half the day as a borrowing and half the day as a hire. The two cows were given for half a day of borrowing and half a day of hire.
the lender says, "during the borrowing time both died". And he claims from the borrower payment for both.
one died during its borrowing and the other I do not know. So he admits part of the claim, and is obligated to swear by Torah law as one who admits part of a claim (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:1).

since he cannot swear, he must pay for both. Because he does not know when the second cow died, he cannot swear that he is exempt from paying for it, and in an oath by Torah law the rule is that one who cannot swear pays.
two borrowed and one hired. And two of the three cows died.
this law will be explained in Hilchot To'en VeNit'an etc.. See Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 4:7-8.
and how do they pay?. Before the defendant pays, he may place a ban on anyone who makes a claim against him that is not certain (ibid. halakhah 7).

and for what reason do they pay?. In Hilchot To'en VeNit'an no explicit reason is found for this principle. One may say that one who is obligated to take an oath by Torah law is not released from paying the claim unless he swears, and if he does not swear, they go down to his property and collect the payment from him (ibid. 1:4) - therefore if he cannot swear, he must pay.

and it was stolen from the man's house etc.. Before this it says: "If a man gives his neighbor money or vessels to keep," and the Sages learned that this passage speaks of an unpaid custodian, who is exempt for theft and loss (Bavli, Bava Metzia 94b).

and the master of the house shall come near to God. The Sages explained that "God" stated here is a term for judges, and that this approach is the oath administered to the custodian regarding his claim (ibid. 41b).

and they extend the oath to him etc.. Besides the basic oath that the deposit was stolen or lost and is not in his possession, the oath is extended to include that the theft or loss was not caused by his negligence in guarding, and that he did not lay a hand on the deposit before it was stolen or lost (compare below 6:1).

for if it was stolen after he laid a hand on the deposit, he is liable for its responsibility. From the moment he took the deposit to bring it into his own domain or used it for his own needs, he has the law of a robber and is liable for the object in every case (see Hilchot Gezelah 3:11).
what is the way of custodians?. What degree of guarding of the deposit is required, such that if he did not guard at that level he is called negligent.
in a gatehouse. The entrance room of a house.

such as beams and stones. Although the gatehouse is a place where people pass by, items like these, which because of their weight and size are not stolen easily and without notice, are guarded in this way.
in a chest. A cabinet.

even if it was lost there by circumstances beyond control... he is negligent and must pay. For anything that begins in negligence, even if it ends in circumstances beyond control, he is liable (as below halakhah 6).
with his own he is permitted, but with others' he is not permitted. His own money he may guard as he sees fit, but others' money he must guard in the proper manner of guarding.
silver coins. Silver coins.
and denarii. Gold denarii.
on the beams of the roof. On the roof beam.
some of the discerning ruled. Those who derive one matter from another and compare cases that share a common principle.
for anything whose carrying is light. And it is easy for thieves to remove it from the custodian's domain.
and the ground does not quickly destroy it. It is not spoiled by the dampness of the ground when it is buried there temporarily.
tongues of silver. Silver ingots, elongated pieces of molten silver.
and needless to say tongues of gold and precious stones. Which are not spoiled by the ground.
Friday at twilight. Close to the time of the Sabbath's entry, when he is busy with Sabbath preparations and has no time to bury them in the ground.
and if he delayed until the departure of the Sabbath for the time needed to bury them. If at the departure of the Sabbath he delayed for a time sufficient to bury the money.

and if he is a Torah scholar he is not liable until he delays long enough to bury them after he makes Havdalah. If the custodian is a Torah scholar who is careful to find wine for Havdalah and to make Havdalah over the cup himself, and this caused him to delay burying the money, he is not liable (some read "and if the depositor is a Torah scholar", and therefore the custodian delayed burying the money in case the depositor needed the money to buy wine for Havdalah - see Ra'avad and Maggid Mishneh).
bound and placed in his hand or tied on his belly in front of his face. Placed in a closed purse held in his hand, or tied on the front of his body so that he can see them.
in a fence of reeds. A wall made of dense reeds.

and anything that begins in negligence and ends in circumstances beyond control, he is liable. If he was negligent with it and did not guard it properly in one respect, even though in the end it was lost by circumstances beyond control in another respect, he is considered negligent and must pay. And the liability applies only if the circumstances beyond control might have been avoided had he not been negligent (such as in the case discussed here, where had he put it elsewhere it might not have been stolen). But if the circumstances beyond control would have occurred in any case (such as if he was negligent in guarding an animal and in the end it died regardless of how it was guarded), he is exempt even though he was negligent at first (see Hilchot Sechirut 3:10).
he is negligent. Knowing where the deposit is placed is part of the duty of guarding, and one who does not know is negligent.
with the understanding of his wife etc.. On the understanding that the custodian could leave the deposit in their care.
or to his slaves. Even a Hebrew slave (Meiri, Bava Metzia 42b).
who do not dwell with him in the house and rely on his table. Who are not part of the household and do not depend on the householder's table.
to another. To a stranger.

unless the second custodian brought proof that he was not negligent. When there are witnesses that the second custodian guarded properly and the object was lost by circumstances beyond his control, the first custodian is released (but if there are no witnesses, the second custodian cannot swear that it was lost by circumstances beyond control, because the owners can claim that they do not believe his oath).
as we have explained. Hilchot Sechirut 1:4.
and did not hide them. In the wall or in the ground.
and even though he did not tell them they were a deposit. And it could be said that this is negligence.
he may claim etc.. He may claim that he did well not to tell her.

the custodian swears that those very coins are what he gave to his mother. To make sure that the coins the depositor claims are the ones about which the mother swore (Maggid Mishneh in the name of the early authorities; and see Yad Pashut, who explained otherwise).
hops. A plant used to make beer.

and he thought he was showing him a place and was not particular about it. The attendant thought the custodian meant to show him where there were hops, and did not mean for him to take specifically from there.
and he pays only the value of what he benefited. Although from the standpoint of guarding he is exempt, since he profited from the depositor's hops, he pays what he benefited.
therefore if the beer turned to vinegar. The beer turned sour and he did not benefit from the hops.
and either way etc.. In all cases where the custodian is exempt, the exemption applies only if he swears about his claim.
money of the poor. Money designated for distribution to the poor.
and he was negligent with it and it was stolen, he is exempt. Although an unpaid custodian is liable for negligence.

as it is stated "to keep," not to distribute to the poor, and it is money that has no claimants. The depositor cannot claim it because it is not his money, for it is designated for distribution to the poor, and the poor cannot claim it either because it is not designated or fixed for specific poor people.

even if thieves came upon him and he hurried and saved himself with the money of the captives. He gave the thieves money that was designated for redeeming captives so that the thieves would not harm him or take him captive.
there is no redemption of captives greater than this. For he used this money in keeping with its purpose.

but if it was for these poor people or these captives, and it is fixed for them. That the money is designated for the poor of a particular place or city, and the charity collectors cannot change its purpose to the poor of another city (Kesef Mishneh; and the Maggid Mishneh explained that there must also be a defined share for each of the poor).

if he is estimated to be a man of wealth he is liable, for the presumption is that the thieves came because of him. If the custodian is estimated to be wealthy, the thieves came because of his money and not because of the deposit.
and it turns out that he saved himself with his fellow's money. And one who saves himself with his fellow's money must pay (see Hilchot Chovel UMazik 8:2).

and if he is not estimated, the presumption is that they came only on hearing of the deposit. If the custodian is not estimated to be wealthy, it is unlikely that the thieves came for his money, but rather for the deposit placed with him.

since he did not cry out, he is negligent. Even calling for help is within the guarding responsibility of an unpaid custodian. His duty is to call for help free of charge, but if he could not find anyone to help him except for pay, he is exempt (see Hilchot Sechirut 3:6).
and one of them died and he does not know whose it was. And he does not know to whom he must return the living animal and to whom the carcass.
he pays both. After they swear (Meiri, Bava Metzia 37b).

and if they deposited with his flock without his knowledge. The shepherd agreed to guard, but the owners put the animals into the flock in his absence, and he could not see to whom each belonged (Tosafot there).
he places the animal between them and withdraws. He places the animal with the court or in the hand of a third party, and does not need to pay both (Meiri there).
and the custodian says, "I do not know". Who deposited the two hundred.

by the law of every one who swears and takes. The Sages enacted that in certain cases where there is no oath obligation by Torah law, the claimant may swear on his claim and collect from the defendant (although normally it is the defendant who swears to be released from the claim against him), and this oath is taken while holding a Torah scroll (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:2).
in one bundle. Bound together.
or until he admits to his fellow. The one who deposited the hundred.
I did not trouble myself to know and always remember the owner of the hundred from the owner of the two hundred. Who is the owner of the hundred and who is the owner of the two hundred.

and from the larger he gives the value of the smaller to the second. If it is a vessel such that when a piece is cut from it the piece has value and so does what remains of the vessel, he gives him an actual piece of the vessel equal in value to the smaller vessel. If not, he gives one of them monetary value equal to the smaller vessel, and the larger vessel remains with him (Meiri, Bava Metzia 37a).
and likewise one whom two claimed etc.. And only one of them deposited with him.

he pays both. After they swear while holding an object, because he was negligent, in that he should have written on the item who the owner of the deposit is (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 3:3).

he may not mix them with his own produce. Because the depositor wants to get back the produce he deposited and not other produce (Gra 292:33 based on Bavli, Bava Metzia 38a), or so that he will know how much produce to return to him if the produce diminishes.

and he should see how much the whole has diminished and calculate the shortage of the deposit. Stored produce tends to shrink and diminish over time for various reasons, and he must calculate the depositor's produce shortage in proportion to the shortage of all the produce in order to know how much produce he must return to him.
and give it to him after he swears. He must swear the custodians' oath that the produce diminished for a natural reason and not because of negligence and the like.

he used some of it and does not know how much he used. He took produce from the mixture for his own needs and does not know how much, and now it is impossible to calculate how much the deposit's produce diminished relative to all the produce.

he deducts shortages for him. He reduces from the produce he returns to the depositor the shortage according to the accepted measure, in line with the produce of the region and its climate and what is known among people who store produce and grain (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 3:7).
for wheat and peeled rice, four and a half kav per kor. For every kor of wheat or rice he receives as a deposit, he returns a kor minus four and a half kav (a kor is one hundred eighty kav).
and by this measure for each and every year. For each year the deposit is with him he deducts these amounts, since with the passing of time the loss or scattering of produce increases.

that he measured to him in the days of the threshing floor and returned to him in the days of the threshing floor. That the deposit and the return were at the time the produce is brought to the threshing floor, while it is dry.

he does not deduct shortages for him because they increase. Because the grain absorbs moisture over time and its volume increases, and when he returns it by the same volume measure the shrinkage is already accounted for (and see Penei Yehoshua, Bava Metzia 40a, who explained otherwise).

and likewise he deducts a sixth for wine. When he deposited wine with him and he mixed it with his own wine and used the mixture, he returns a sixth less than the amount he received because of the jars' absorption of the wine and because of evaporation.

of which a log and a half is lees and a log and a half is absorption. Of the three logs deducted, a log and a half is for the lees that settle at the bottom of the jar, and a log and a half for what is absorbed in the jar.
if it was refined oil. Oil that was strained from its dregs.
and if the jars were old he does not deduct absorption for him. For the jars already absorbed all they need and do not absorb more.
produce that was not measured. Whose quantity or weight was not measured.
he was negligent. He should have measured it before mixing it with his own produce, and since he did not measure it, he is defined as negligent and must pay.

and he turns out to be obligated to swear and cannot swear. For the custodian admits that he owes him produce but does not know how much, so he is considered as admitting part of the claim and is obligated to swear by Torah law. But since he does not know how much was deposited with him, he cannot swear against the depositor's claim, and the rule is that anyone who is obligated to swear and cannot swear, pays (see also Hilchot Chovel UMazik 7:19).
my teachers ruled, Rabbi Yosef HaLevi. Rabbi Yosef ibn Migash (see his novellae to Shevuot 43a).
and his teacher. The Rif (see Responsa of the Rif, Rothstein edition, no. 46).
provided that they claim something for which they are estimated. The claimant is believed only if he claims a reasonable amount based on the estimate of his wealth.
and the custodian may place a ban etc.. The custodian may place a ban in court, so that the depositor will refrain from a false claim (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:4 and the commentary there).
consider for yourself. Try to understand.
as will be explained. Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 4:7-8.

that the custodian swears by enactment of the Sages that it is not in his possession. As with every custodian, in cases where he must pay, the Sages enacted that he swear while holding an object that the deposit is not in his possession (as below 6:1).

and he includes in his oath that he does not know for certain that it was worth more than such and such. He includes in his oath that it is clear to him that the deposit's value was not more than a certain amount.
and he pays what he admits. Since the claimant too does not make a certain claim about the deposit's value, the custodian pays according to the value he admitted in his oath.
jewelry. A piece of jewelry.
alloys. A mixture of metals.

provided that he claims something for which he is estimated, or that he was estimated to deposit with him. That it is reasonable to say that the claimant owned such things or deposited them with him for guarding (see also Hilchot Chovel UMazik 7:18).

and why does the owner of the deposit swear here?. For when the custodian admits that he received the deposit and does not know its value, the depositor collects without an oath (as above halakhah 6), so why here must he swear to collect?

because the custodian is not obligated to swear etc.. For if he were obligated to swear by Torah law and could not swear, he would pay without an oath by the owner of the deposit; but in this case the custodian is not admitting part of the claim so as to be obligated to swear by Torah law, since even if he made a certain claim about what he said, he would swear a lesser oath (hesset) and be released.

like one whom he claimed wheat and he admitted barley. One who admits part is not obligated to swear unless he admitted part of the claimant's claim, and not if he admitted part of a different type of claim.
and in Hilchot To'en VeNit'an. 3:8-10.

an unpaid custodian who said, "I will pay and I will not swear". He claims that the deposit was stolen from him and the like, but does not want to swear to this and be released from paying, preferring to pay the owner for the deposit.
something all of whose kind is equal in value. That all items of the same type as the deposit are equal to one another.
we suspect that perhaps he set his eyes on it. Perhaps the deposit was not lost, but the custodian coveted it for himself and wants to pay the owners and keep the deposit in his possession.
and if the owners said, "it was worth more than this". More than the value the custodian admits.
he includes in his oath that it is worth only such and such. He extends his oath to include this detail too.
every custodian who swears the custodians' oath. If he makes a claim that exempts him and is obligated to swear by Torah law.
that he guarded in the manner of custodians. That he was not negligent in guarding.

and that such and such happened to it and it is not in his possession. The custodian swears about the circumstances that befell the deposit because of which the object left his possession. This is the main part of the oath (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 8:2, and see above 4:1).
and that he did not lay a hand on it etc.. For if he laid a hand on it he became a robber and is liable for the deposit in every case (see above 4:1).
and he includes in his oath that it was worth such and such. In a case where there is no agreement on the deposit's value.
the custodian may stipulate. The custodian may make a condition.
I will place them in a corner of my house. In the corner of the house, and not in the ground as money must be guarded (above 4:4).
and the like. He may stipulate in advance for any deviation from the usual.
for we had a stipulation between us. And according to the stipulation he is exempt from paying.
an unpaid custodian who brought proof that he was not negligent. Rather, he guarded the object properly, and the object was stolen or lost without his negligence.

and we do not say perhaps he laid a hand on it before it was lost. For an oath about laying a hand is extended to him in addition to the basic custodians' oath (above 4:1). And since here he is exempt from the basic oath, this oath is not extended to him.
and if he claimed and said, "we had a stipulation between us". And according to the stipulation he is exempt for negligence.

that he deposited this object before us with him. The witnesses now see the object in the custodian's hand and testify that this object was given to him as a deposit (for if they did not see the object in the custodian's hand, he is believed in his claim that he later bought it or received it as a gift, since he could claim that he returned the object - Maggid Mishneh).
and said, "I deposited such and such". And he has no witnesses to this.
distinguishing signs. For example, he gave the weight of the deposit (see below, and see Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 13:5).
for the deceased was not estimated to own this deposit. According to the estimate of his wealth, it is not reasonable that the object belonged to him.
and he recognized its signs. When he entered, he noticed the signs of the deposit.
witnesses came and testified to the judge that he is not estimated. The judge did not know the deceased, but witnesses testify that he is not estimated to have owned the deposit.
for this is not clear proof. Since they are not testifying to facts they saw, but only to their estimate.

and the judge has only what his own mind relies on. A judge has authority to rule and extract money on the basis of his own estimate even without clear proof from witnesses, but he cannot rely on the estimate of others.

as I will explain in Hilchot Sanhedrin. 24:1. Although in halakhah 2 there Maimonides wrote that this is the main law, at a later stage most courts agreed that a judge should not rely on his own estimate, because many courts are not upright or wise enough.
sesame. Sesame seeds.
and is not their measure such and such?. He told him their quantity, and it turned out as he said.
while holding an object. A severe oath, rabbinic in origin.
as we have explained. Hilchot Sechirut 2:12.
it was new and you used it. And its value decreased as a result.
and the householder says, "this is the very one you deposited, and what you gave you take". The custodian claims that what is before him is what was deposited with him and no more.

he swears a lesser oath like all other defendants. Like any defendant who denies the entire claim against him (as explained in Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:3). In this case he is not obligated in the oath of one who admits part, since to obligate him to this he must explicitly admit a defined quantity (Beit Yosef 296, and see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 4:1).

when he admits to the very deposit as the depositor says etc.. There is no doubt what he deposited with him, only what happened afterward and whether he is liable for it. In this case they swear the custodians' oath as explained at the beginning of the chapter.
or an oath by Torah law if he admitted part. Like any defendant who admits part, who is obligated to swear by Torah law about what he denies.

he swears a lesser oath like all others who swear on such a claim. Since he did not admit part of the kind the claimant claimed, he is not in the category of one who admits part (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 3:8).
he may not touch them even though they are shrinking, diminishing and going. A person prefers a little of his own to a lot of another's (Bavli, Bava Metzia 38a).
the shortage proper to them each year. See above 5:5.
because of returning a lost item to its owners. For there is the commandment of returning a lost item to its owners.
at the price of terumah. At the price of terumah produce, which is lower than ordinary produce.

perhaps the owners made it terumah or terumat ma'aser on other produce. Perhaps the produce he deposited was tevel (untithed), and the depositor had other tevel produce of the same kind, and in order to eat it he designated the deposited produce as terumah on the produce in his possession.
a benefit for the owner of the deposit. An action for the depositor's benefit.
spreads. Spreads out.
the jars and vessels add loss. The longer wine is left in the vessels after they have spoiled, the greater the damage caused to the vessels.
until the fifth hour of the fourteenth. The fifth hour of the morning on the 14th of Nisan, when leaven is forbidden to eat but permitted for benefit, so he can sell it to a gentile.

he goes out and sells it in the market at its time. He must sell the leaven immediately (and so this expression is explained elsewhere - see Yad Pashut). For if he waits until the beginning of the sixth hour, the leaven becomes forbidden for benefit by rabbinic law, and it will be impossible to sell it (Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 1:9).

he rolls it once in twelve months. So that it will not become moldy and spoil (and although Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 13:13 says one who finds a book must roll it once in thirty days, for a deposit deposited with the owner's knowledge the Sages did not burden the custodian to do so, since if the depositor wanted this he would have told the custodian explicitly - Meiri, Bava Metzia 29b).
he opened it and read in it, it is permitted. Since he rolled it for the deposit's sake, they permitted him to read in it as well while doing so.
for his own sake. For his own need.
he has laid a hand on the deposit and become liable for its circumstances beyond control. Above 4:1.
a garment. A garment.
in the way that was said regarding a lost item etc.. See Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 13:11-13, where the ways of handling various lost items are detailed.
in what case does this apply? etc.. All the laws stated from the beginning of the chapter until here apply when the owners are not present.
but if they were with him in the same land he may not touch it. Rather, he informs the owners and they decide what to do with it.
because of suspicion. That people will say he sold to himself cheaply.
and he may. He is permitted.
he is a paid custodian over them even though he has not yet used them. The very permission to use is payment for his guarding.
if they were bundled. Gathered in a purse and the like.
and sealed. A seal was impressed on the mouth of the bundle to ensure it was not opened.
tied with an unusual knot. A knot different from the usual, so that the depositor can know whether it was untied.
he may not use them. The seal or knot prove that he does not want the bundle opened.
he may use them. Since it is the way of a shopkeeper and a money changer to use money, presumably the depositor agrees that they be used, unless there is evidence that he does not agree.
therefore. Since he has permission to use them.
by an armed robber. An armed bandit.

he is liable for their responsibility like any loan in the world etc.. Since the money does not remain in his hand, he has not the law of a custodian but of a borrower of money, who is liable in every case until he repays the loan.

one who deposits money with a householder... he may not use it. Since he does not deal in money, it is reasonable that the owner of the money deposited it on the understanding that he would not use it.
provided that he buries it in the ground. For that is the way of guarding it.
as we have explained. Above 4:4.
for which the owners designated a place. They agreed in advance that it would be placed in a particular place.
and he moved it for his own need. To make a certain use of it for himself.
from his hand. While it was still in his hand before he put it down.
he must pay. Since he moved it for his own need he is considered as laying a hand on the deposit and is liable for it.
he moved it for its own sake. To protect it and the like.
exempt. Since he was not negligent.

we do not accept deposits from women, nor from slaves, nor from minors. Presumably they have no property of their own, and there is concern that they stole the item from the husband, the master, or the father. Therefore we do not accept from them, so that they will return the item to the place from which they took it (Yad Ramah, Bava Batra 51b).
if he accepted from a woman, he returns to the woman etc.. Despite the concern that it is not theirs, it is possible that they received it from someone else and did not steal it.
if he accepted from a minor, he buys with it a Torah scroll etc.. He does not return the deposit to him, for fear he will lose it, but buys with it long-term property for the minor.

if they are believed by him, he does as they specified, and if not, he returns to their heirs. After their death their property passes to their heirs, so he does as they said only if their words are credible to him, and if not, he gives the deposit to the heirs. But during their lifetime he returns it to them, and they may give the deposit to whom they say the item belongs (Rabbi Yosef ibn Migash in Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Batra 52a).
and if he returned his deposit to him in Nov, he accepts it from him. Although the depositor cannot make a claim in another place, the custodian may return it to him in another place.
he does not accept it from him. He is not obligated to accept it.
to set sail. To sail across the sea.
who ruled. Who decided.
in the hand of one trusted by them etc.. In the hands of a person who is trusted by them, to take care of the deposit.
or they were lost... and the thief was found. For example, the custodian thought the deposit was lost, but in the end it became clear that it was stolen (Tosafot, Bava Metzia 33b).

and said, "I will pay," and did not want to swear etc.. By the basic law he could swear to this and be exempt from paying, like an unpaid custodian (and this refers even to a case where he only said he would pay but has not actually paid - see below halakhah 2).
slaughtered or sold, he pays the payments of four and five. One who steals an ox or sheep and slaughters or sells it pays four times for the sheep and five times for the ox (Hilchot Genevah 1:16).
to the one with whom the deposit was. The custodian.

for he said, "I will pay". The deposit was made on the understanding that if the deposit were stolen and the custodian volunteered to pay for it, the deposit would be acquired by the custodian, and therefore the thief pays everything to the custodian (see Bavli, Bava Metzia 34a).

if the animal itself returned, it returns to its owners etc.. When the custodian volunteers to pay the value of the deposit and acquires it, he does not acquire the profits that come from the body of the deposit, such as fleece and offspring of an animal, but only the gain that comes from outside (such as double payment or gain from the rise in price of the deposit, as below 5:3).
and we have already explained. Hilchot Genevah 1:11.
that the thief returns fleece and offspring only before despair. And the discussion here is only about gain before despair.
the custodian swore etc.. This is the basic law written in the Torah (Exodus 22:7), that the custodian is released by an oath and the depositor receives all the payments.
and likewise the hirer. Who has the law of a paid custodian and is liable for theft and loss (Hilchot Sechirut 1:2).
was identified. Was recognized, found.

but the borrower does not acquire the double payment until he pays of his own accord. It is not enough that he says he will pay, for the borrower benefits from the object, using it free of charge, and for this reason the owner grants him the double payment only when he actually pays for the stolen object (Bavli, Bava Metzia 34a).
whoever acquires the double acquires the gain that comes on its own. Gain that does not come from the body of the deposit (see above halakhah 1).
and they were worth four sela'im. Until they were found, their value rose fourfold.
it returns to the owners as it is. The owners receive the deposit and acquire the double payment or the profit due to its rise in price.

and if vessels or land, the court collected from him by appraisal. If the custodian had no money to pay, and the court collected from his property something equal in value to the deposit and gave it to the depositor.
and he swore and afterward paid. After he swore and was released from paying, he decided to pay anyway beyond the letter of the law.
and then said again, "I will pay," he acquired the double. Since he agreed to pay of his own accord.

he said "I will pay," and then said "I will not pay," or said "I will pay" and died and the sons said "we will not pay". In these cases there is doubt whether to rely on the initial agreement and see the second statement as only a temporary postponement of payment, or whether this is a retraction of the agreement to pay and he did not acquire the theft payments (Bavli, Bava Metzia 34b).

or he did not manage to claim... or the sons paid the sons. And there is doubt whether the payments are granted also to the custodian's sons, or only to the custodian, since he both accepted the guarding and paid (ibid.).

or the custodian paid half; he borrowed two cows and paid for one of them. And there is doubt whether he grants him the theft payments corresponding to the half he paid, or does not grant them until he pays everything.
borrowed from partners and paid one of them. For his share in the partnership.
partners who borrowed and one paid. For his share in the joint borrowing.
borrowed from the woman. From her melog property, whose fruits the husband is entitled to.

and paid her husband. Theft payments for melog property are given to the husband since they are like fruits, and there is doubt whether paying the husband and not the wife is enough to acquire them (Meiri, ibid.).
a woman who borrowed and her husband paid. And there is doubt whether the lender treats her husband's payment as if she had paid him and grants her the theft payments.
and if one of them got ahead and seized everything, we do not take it from his hand. For we do not extract money on the basis of doubt.

even outside the Land. Where fines are not adjudicated, and the thief is exempt from the double, fourfold and fivefold payments, which are fines; nevertheless, if one of them already seized, we do not extract it from his hand (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:13, ibid. halakhah 17).
he litigates with the thief and does not swear. See rulings and views.
got ahead and swore. And was released.
if he wishes he stands on his oath etc.. He may rely on having sworn and been released, and is not obligated to litigate with the thief.
and it is an animal. The deposit is an animal.
and if the owners seized. From the custodian's property in order to collect the value of the deposit.

we do not take it from their hands. Since they are now in possession of the money, and we do not extract money on the basis of doubt, as perhaps he really was obligated to pay them and they hold his money lawfully.
